m.i.title: megamesh.sh — Your server, your exit.
m.i.description: Megamesh turns the cheapest VPS into a hardened personal WireGuard VPN with a web admin. Three open ports, key-only SSH, fail2ban, automatic TLS, weekly health-checked upgrades with rollback. Script, AI prompt, or one-click deployer. Open source, MIT.
m.i.og_description: A hardened personal WireGuard VPN on a 1 GB VPS. Script for sysops, prompt for AI agents, a web deployer for everyone else. Open source, MIT.
i.008: Your own VPN · one IP and root away
i.010: Megamesh turns the cheapest VPS you can rent into a hardened personal WireGuard VPN with a web admin for your devices. Three open ports, key-only SSH, automatic TLS, weekly upgrades that roll back on their own. Yours, auditable, MIT.
i.020: Renting a tunnel, you're a subscriber. Running one, you're the operator. Commercial VPNs were built for scale, not for you: a shared exit, a privacy policy you take on faith, a box you will never see. Most self-hosting guides stop at “WireGuard is up” and leave the door open. Megamesh is the rest of the job — hardened by default, on a VPS that costs less than the subscription.
i.023: One bash file you can read in ten minutes, a prompt for your AI agent, and the configs running on the reference server — published whole, MIT, audited twice by three frontier models with every finding and what was done about it.
i.025: Idempotent, non-interactive, every setting an environment variable. Re-running keeps your choices.
i.027: PROMPT.md carries the goal, the safety rules and the six traps we hit, so the agent starts at the end.
i.029: IP, root password, domain, email. It changes the root password to one you choose, installs, and hands over your admin login.
i.036:
Three doors.
Everything else is a wall.
i.037: The public internet reaches exactly three ports. The firewall's default is DROP, not reject: scanners get silence. Inside, two containers and a handful of host settings — all written down, none of them clever.
i.040: tcp/22, udp/51820, tcp/443 and nothing else. No port 80, no admin port, no Docker ports leaking through. ICMP limited to ping and path-MTU.
i.042: Password login stays on until a key is proven to work, then goes away. Three tries, 24 h bans doubling to 30 days. 76,073 attempts became a handful of addresses.
i.044: Caddy terminates 443 with Let's Encrypt over TLS-ALPN — no port 80 ever opens. HSTS, strict headers, Server header stripped.
i.047: Peers, QR codes, stats, 2FA. The UI port is never published; the admin account is created unattended before 443 is reachable, so nobody can race you to the wizard.
i.050: topgrade pulls packages and container images, restarts, verifies the tunnel is up and the admin answers — or rolls back to the images that worked. Pinned by SHA-256.
i.053: One command makes the admin page answer only through the tunnel; outsiders get a 302 to any URL you choose. Certificates keep renewing.
i.056: No wizard, no questions. The installer runs the same five stages every time and refuses to open a door it cannot prove you can walk through.
i.058: Swap, hostname, kernel modules the container will need.
i.060: Full system update, Docker from the signed repo, daily automatic updates on.
i.062: Firewall first, then sshd, fail2ban, sysctl. Never lock before the firewall is open.
i.064: wg-easy alone, admin account proven, only then Caddy. Fails closed.
i.066: Handshake, ports, certificate retry, timers. Then it hands you the credentials.
i.067: failed SSH logins the reference server took in 25 days before Megamesh — with fail2ban “running” and zero jails. After: a handful of banned addresses, and silence.
i.068: Typical VPS image, untouched<small>ports answering from the internet</small>
i.069: Guide-followed WireGuard box<small>wg + ssh + web + docker leaks</small>
i.073: A personal VPN changes who can see your traffic, not whether anyone can. The repository says exactly what has and has not been exercised.
i.075: Your VPS provider sees your traffic leave their network. Megamesh hides you from the café Wi-Fi and your ISP, not from a subpoena.
i.077: One admin, your devices. wg-easy supports many peers, but the hardening assumes a single trusted operator.
i.079: It changes your root password but leaves SSH on a password until someone installs a key, and leaves 2FA and VPN-only mode for you to switch on. Twenty minutes with the hardening notes finishes it.
i.081: CentOS Stream 9 and Ubuntu 24.04 on a 1 vCPU / 1 GB VPS are verified end to end — the second one through the deployer itself. Rocky, Alma and Debian share those code paths but have not been run yet.
i.084: Once your devices are on the tunnel, everything you do leaves from your server's address. That is the point — and a fact others can use: a friend can allow-list you, your own boxes can trust you, a rate limit can make an exception. The author publishes his, and the repository is the source of truth for it.
i.111: Publishing it is also a defence. Calumny, fake news, a “someone broke into our app” accusation — every action on the internet leaves an address in a log. Declare yours in public, with a start date, and any trace that comes from somewhere else is, by your own prior declaration, not you. It does not prove innocence by itself, but it gives you leverage: a public, dated, verifiable statement made before anyone had a reason to doubt it.
i.089: Verifydig +short A paulfleury.network · dig +short -x 151.243.225.214 — they must agree
i.090: It identifies a server, not a person. Keep authentication in front of whatever you allow-list — and the address had other tenants before the start date; nothing from before it is the author's.
i.093: Megamesh is the single-person version of the boxes megastack.sh, the author's cybersecurity consultancy, builds for clients — designed and operated with an AI agent over SSH, then torn apart by three other models before going public.
i.094: Paul Fleury — French internet entrepreneur in Lisbon, hacking around on the internet since the late nineties.
i.095: The whole story — the logbook of the first deployment, the audits, the fixes — is in the repository.
i.113: Your server, your exit. One script, three open ports, nothing stored with us.
i.096: megamesh.sh · MIT · Megamesh is a word, megamesh.sh is a command
m.d.title: Deploy Megamesh on your VPS · megamesh.sh
m.d.description: Give the deployer your VPS IP, root password, domain and email. It changes the root password to one you choose, installs Megamesh and hands over with your admin credentials.
d.008: Four things, then wait. The deployer logs into your server over SSH, changes the root password to one you choose, installs Megamesh exactly as the public script would, and comes back with your admin login. Nothing you type is stored anywhere — it lives in this tab and in the requests that carry it.
d.014: A fresh VPS with CentOS Stream 9 or Ubuntu 24.04 (both verified end to end, including through this page) — Rocky/Alma 9 and Debian 12 may work but are not yet tested. 1 vCPU and 1 GB of RAM are enough. You need root over SSH with a password, and a domain whose DNS you can edit.
d.017: Current root password <small>from your provider's email or panel</small>
d.019: The one your provider sent has already travelled by email. The deployer replaces it on the server before installing anything, and uses the new one from then on. Save it in your password manager now; it is shown again at hand-over.
d.020: New root password <small>12–128 characters, no spaces — or leave empty to keep the current one</small>
d.024: Your SSH public key <small>optional — if you have one, it goes in and the box is fully hardened</small>
d.025: Read before you click. Your root password is sent over HTTPS to megamesh.sh, used to log into your server for the duration of the install, and discarded. Each status refresh logs in again with it. We keep no copy and no logs of it. If you would rather not, the script gives the same result without us in the middle.
d.028: Logged in. Here is what the deployer found, and what it is about to do.
d.029: I understand that the install takes 10–30 minutes, that my root password transits through megamesh.sh during that time and is not stored, and that SSH stays password-protected until a key is installed.
d.033: Package updates on a 1 vCPU box take a while — 10 to 30 minutes is normal. You can leave this tab open; the install continues on your server even if you close it, and re-opening the deployer with the same details picks it back up.
d.042: Three things left, all on your side. Save the credentials first — they are shown once.
d.043: Point your domain at the server. At your DNS provider (Namecheap, Cloudflare, OVH…), create an A record: host @, value . Remove any parking or redirect record on the same name. Caddy on your server is already waiting and will fetch a certificate by itself once the record resolves — usually within minutes.
d.044: Log in. Open (type the https://), sign in with the admin credentials above, then enable two-factor authentication under your account. Add a device, scan the QR code, connect.
d.045: Have a techie friend finish the hardening — twenty minutes with the hardening notes: install an SSH key and turn passwords off, optionally make the admin page VPN-only. Everything else (firewall, fail2ban, automatic updates, weekly health-checked upgrades) is already running.
d.046: Credentials on the server. A copy of the admin login sits in /root/megamesh-admin-credentials on your VPS, readable by root only. Once you have saved everything in a password manager, remove it:
d.047: I saved them — delete the copy on the server
d.062: Your server, your exit. One script, three open ports, nothing stored with us.
j.lang.title: Choose your language
j.lang.note: Translated by machine from the English original, which stays the reference — technical terms and the terminal stay in English. Your choice is remembered on this device.
j.lang.empty: No language matches that. Try the English name.
j.d.err_ip: Enter the server's public IPv4 address, like 203.0.113.10.
j.d.err_pw: The current root password is required.
j.d.err_domain: Enter a full domain name, like vpn.example.com.
j.d.err_pubkey: One line, starting with ssh-ed25519 or ssh-rsa.
j.d.mm_installed: already installed — running again is safe
j.d.ssh_key: your key is installed; password login stays on until you turn it off
j.d.ssh_nokey: password login stays on (no key given)
j.d.note_unsupported: Unsupported system. The installer knows CentOS Stream / Rocky / Alma 9 and Debian / Ubuntu on x86_64. Reinstall the VPS with CentOS Stream 9 or Ubuntu 24.04 from your provider's panel and try again.
j.d.note_finished: A finished install is waiting for you. The credentials file is still on the server — the button below reads it and shows the hand-over, nothing is installed again.
j.d.note_running: An install is already running on this server. Installing will attach to it rather than start another.
j.d.note_besteffort: Best-effort system. Only CentOS Stream 9 and Ubuntu 24.04 have been verified end to end; this one takes a code path that has not been run yet. It will probably work — if it fails, the log will say where.
j.d.note_small: Small box. Under 1 GB visible RAM; the installer adds swap before updating, which is exactly the case it was built for.
j.d.stopped_hint: The install stopped with an error.
j.d.stopped_err: The last lines above say where. Fix the cause (or reinstall the VPS) and run the deployer again — the installer is idempotent.
j.d.log_started: Connected. {pw}Installer started on your server — downloading the release and updating packages…
j.d.pw_changed_note: (Note: the root password HAS been changed to the new one you chose.)
j.d.h_account_earlier: was created on an earlier run — use the credentials you saved then
j.d.h_read_failed: Installed, but reading the credentials failed: {msg}. On the server: cat /root/megamesh-admin-credentials
j.d.forgot: Deleted from the server. Only your password manager has them now.
